issues.legal_issue: A written agreement that immediately varies mortgage terms and thereby limits or extinguishes the mortgagee’s interest in the mortgaged property requires registration.
material_facts: The dispute was a suit to recover money due under two mortgages.
The mortgagee executed a written agreement in favour of the mortgagor that stated it was settling new terms for the mortgage transactions.
The agreement reduced the interest rate provided in the mortgages and prescribed payment terms under which the mortgage transactions would be treated as fully paid.
The agreement stated that no interest remained claimable and that the principal had been fully paid.
issues.conclusion: The agreement itself limited or extinguished an interest in immovable property and required registration under section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, a written instrument that by its own force limits or extinguishes an interest in immovable property must be registered. A mortgagee’s right to receive interest at the rate specified in the mortgage forms part of the mortgagee’s interest; changing that rate by a subsequent agreement limits or creates an interest. The agreement is distinguished from a receipt that merely records payment made under the mortgage, because the payment, rather than the receipt, changes the outstanding liability. The Court relied on U. Po Thin v. Official Assignee and referred to Tika Ram v. Deputy Commissioner of Bara Banki; it distinguished the reasoning advanced from Mahim Chandra Dey v. Ram Dayal Dutta, Ram Ranjan v. Jayantilal and Collector of Etah v. Kishori Lal.

rule.if: mortgage_enforcement_suit and later_written_agreement and agreement_itself_changes_mortgage_terms and change_limits_or_extinguishes_mortgage_interest

predicates.mortgage_enforcement_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking recovery of money due under a mortgage.
predicates.later_written_agreement: The mortgagee executed a written agreement with the mortgagor after the mortgage was made.
predicates.agreement_itself_changes_mortgage_terms: The written agreement establishes changed mortgage terms by its own force rather than merely recording an external event.
predicates.change_limits_or_extinguishes_mortgage_i: The changed terms reduce or extinguish an interest the mortgagee could claim under the mortgage.

issues.definition: When a mortgage-recovery suit involves a later written agreement that itself changes mortgage terms and limits or extinguishes the mortgagee’s interest, the agreement requires registration.

issues.legal_issue: A written agreement that itself takes immediate effect in varying mortgage terms is not exempt from registration merely because it also provides for a further document to be executed later.
material_facts: The agreement stated that its new terms were being settled in the present and altered the interest and payment terms of the mortgages.
It also stated that, if the mortgagor wished or necessity arose, the mortgagee would provide the agreement written on stamped paper and registered.
The further registered document was to repeat the agreement already having effect, rather than bring the alteration into effect for the first time.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was not exempt from registration under section 17(2)(v) of the Registration Act because it itself immediately limited or extinguished interests in the mortgaged property and did more than create a right to obtain another document.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(2)(v) of the Registration Act applies where a document merely creates a right to obtain another document that will create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish an interest in immovable property. It does not exempt a document that itself has that effect, even if it contemplates a further document. The Court also relied on the distinction between a present agreement that itself effects the change and an agreement to execute a future transfer document, and referred to Mulla’s statement on the statutory exception.

predicates.mortgage_enforcement_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking recovery of money due under a mortgage.
predicates.written_agreement_itself_effective_now: The written agreement purports to change the parties’ rights immediately by its own terms.
predicates.further_document_only_repeats_or_records: Any further document contemplated by the agreement would repeat or record terms that are already in effect, rather than first create those terms.

issues.definition: If a mortgage-related written agreement itself immediately changes the parties’ rights and a contemplated further document would only repeat or record that change, the agreement is not exempt as a document merely creating a right to obtain another document.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered agreement cannot be used under the collateral-purpose proviso to prove the very agreement that it itself creates when the proceeding is neither for specific performance nor based on part performance.
material_facts: The defendant sought to use the unregistered agreement to prove that the mortgage amounts had been satisfied.
The agreement itself created the altered terms on which the claimed satisfaction depended.
The suit was not for specific performance, and no question of part performance arose.
The agreement was not a transfer, contained no words of conveyance, and the mortgagor’s continued possession was not referable to it.
issues.conclusion: The agreement could not be used under the proviso to section 49 of the Registration Act for the claimed purpose; the claimed use was to prove the agreement itself, not a collateral transaction, and section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to section 49 of the Registration Act does not permit an unregistered document to be used to prove the very transaction that the document itself creates when that transaction requires registration. The collateral-purpose exception does not make the transaction itself collateral. Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act was inapplicable because the agreement was not a transfer and the mortgagor’s possession was not in part performance of it.

rule.if: mortgage_enforcement_suit and unregistered_written_agreement and agreement_itself_creates_transaction and use_seeks_to_prove_same_transaction and not specific_performance_suit and not part_performance_claim

predicates.mortgage_enforcement_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking recovery of money due under a mortgage.
predicates.unregistered_written_agreement: A party seeks to rely on a written agreement that was not registered.
predicates.agreement_itself_creates_transaction: The agreement itself creates the transaction or altered rights that require registration.
predicates.use_seeks_to_prove_same_transaction: The party seeks to use the writing to prove the very transaction it creates, rather than a separate collateral transaction.
predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of the agreement.
predicates.part_performance_claim: A party relies on possession or conduct as part performance of a transfer agreement.

issues.definition: When an unregistered writing itself creates the transaction a party seeks to prove, and the proceeding involves neither specific performance nor part performance, the writing cannot be used for that claimed purpose.
